paragraphs: Jailbreak attacks attempt to make language models produce harmful outputs despite their safeguards. Comparing these attacks requires more than checking whether a model can be manipulated: the settings used for the attack and the defenses applied to the target also matter. This paper introduces JailTrickBench to study those factors within a common evaluation framework.

The benchmark examines eight implementation factors from both the target model and attack perspectives. It evaluates seven representative attacks against six defense methods on two datasets. The reported effort covers approximately 354 experiments and about 55,000 GPU hours, giving the comparison substantial experimental breadth.

The central contribution is a structured basis for evaluating attacks against models with added defenses. The authors report that their results reinforce the need for standardized benchmarking. This matters because conclusions about vulnerability or protection depend on the evaluation setup; a shared framework makes those settings part of the comparison rather than leaving them implicit.
neurips-2024-bag-of-tricks-benchmarking-.tldr: JailTrickBench systematically evaluates jailbreak settings and defenses to support more standardized comparisons of LLM attacks.

paragraphs: Assigning semantic categories to points in a 3D point cloud normally requires extensive annotation. Weak supervision reduces that burden, but leaves the model with fewer signals about how to organize its learned representations. This paper adds guidance by constraining the distribution of those representations, rather than relying only on the available labels.

The authors compare several candidate distributions and identify a mixture of von Mises-Fisher distributions as particularly suitable for the feature space they study. Their Distribution Guidance Network has two branches: one learns from weak supervision, while the other aligns features with the selected distribution. Clustering information from the first branch provides a reliable initialization for the second.

The alignment branch alternates between updating the distribution parameters and updating the network. This lets the distribution model and learned features adjust together. Experiments support both the distribution choice and the architecture, with reported state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and weak supervision settings. The findings show how feature organization can supply useful additional constraints when direct annotation is sparse.
neurips-2024-distribution-guidance-netwo.tldr: DGNet improves weakly supervised point-cloud segmentation by aligning learned features with a fitted mixture distribution.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation lets a pretrained model adjust to incoming data without needing labels for those examples. For vision-language models, existing approaches often adapt only one modality and do not retain task knowledge as more examples arrive. Dual Prototype Evolving addresses both issues by maintaining class representations in text and image form.

The method creates two sets of prototypes, which serve as representative descriptions of the target classes. Both sets evolve during testing, allowing information from successive samples to improve the representations. It also learns residual adjustments for each test sample to bring the textual and visual prototypes into closer alignment.

This design combines accumulated task information with coordination between the two modalities. Across 15 benchmark datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods while retaining competitive computational efficiency. The findings support adapting both sides of a vision-language model and carrying useful information forward through the test sequence, rather than treating adaptation solely as an isolated adjustment to each incoming example.
neurips-2024-dual-prototype-evolving-for.tldr: DPE adapts vision-language models using evolving text and image class prototypes that accumulate knowledge from unlabeled test samples.

paragraphs: A model that answers questions about an entire video may still struggle to identify particular events or locate them in time. E.T. Bench targets this finer level of understanding through open-ended tasks. Its purpose is to assess event-specific abilities that broad video question answering can leave untested.

The benchmark contains 7.3K samples across 12 tasks, organized into a three-level taxonomy. It draws on 7K videos covering eight domains and totaling 251.4 hours. Evaluations of eight image-language models and twelve video-language models show that strong performance on coarse video understanding does not translate reliably to these finer tasks.

The authors attribute much of the difficulty to limited video context, unsuitable time representations, and insufficient training on multiple events. They introduce E.T. Chat and the E.T. Instruct 164K instruction-tuning dataset to address these issues, reporting superior performance in multiple scenarios. Together, the benchmark and baseline make event timing and distinctions between events explicit targets for both evaluation and training.
neurips-2024-e-t-bench-towards-open-ende.tldr: E.T. Bench exposes weaknesses in event-level video understanding and introduces a model and training dataset aimed at those weaknesses.

paragraphs: Articulated objects contain connected parts whose movements are restricted by joints. Estimating their poses is difficult when the object is only partly visible and examples within a category have different structures. EfficientCAPER approaches this problem by making the joints central to pose prediction and removing the need for an optimization stage after the network runs.

Starting from a partial point cloud, the framework first estimates the pose of the object's free part using a decoupled rotation representation. It then transforms the point cloud into a canonical frame. For the constrained parts, it predicts joint parameters and joint states as replacements for directly estimating their poses.

This sequence incorporates the object's movement structure into the prediction process. Evaluations on ArtImage, ReArtMix, and RobotArm support the method's effectiveness, including generalization to real-world scenarios. The reported findings concern static pose estimation: they show that joint-centered modeling can support an efficient end-to-end estimator for partially observed articulated objects across the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2024-efficientcaper-an-end-to-en.tldr: EfficientCAPER estimates articulated-object poses from partial point clouds by predicting joint structure and states without post-processing optimization.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can steer a neural network toward the wrong patterns. Loss functions designed to tolerate this noise can help, but strict symmetry requirements may also prevent effective fitting. This paper proposes epsilon-softmax, a modification to the output layer that relaxes that requirement while retaining control over robustness.

The method makes softmax outputs approximate one-hot vectors, where nearly all of the output is concentrated on one class. A parameter, epsilon, controls the approximation error. Although implemented at the output layer, the change also alters the effective loss function. The authors prove noise-tolerant learning with a controllable excess-risk bound for almost any loss function.

The paper acknowledges a trade-off: losses enhanced this way may fit clean datasets slightly less well. To balance robustness and learning ability, the authors combine them with a symmetric loss. Experiments on synthetic and real-world label noise report superior performance. The contribution links a simple output transformation to theoretical control of noise sensitivity and an empirical strategy for managing reduced fitting ability.
neurips-2024-epsilon-softmax-approximati.tldr: Epsilon-softmax makes predictions nearly one-hot to support noise-tolerant learning, with theoretical risk control and an explicit fitting trade-off.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks involve discrete events alongside continuously evolving states, making their training mathematically challenging when noise affects both. This paper develops a rigorous framework using rough path theory and stochastic differential equations with event discontinuities. It accommodates jumps in both the network's state trajectories and the noise driving them.

The authors identify sufficient conditions under which gradients exist for individual solution paths and event times with respect to network parameters. They also derive a recursive relationship for calculating these gradients. The conditions matter: the result establishes when such differentiation is justified, rather than asserting that every noisy spiking system can be differentiated this way.

For training, the paper introduces a loss based on a new class of signature kernels for paths that can contain jumps, and uses it to train generative spiking models. An automatically differentiable solver is provided through diffrax. The authors describe the framework as, to their knowledge, the first to enable gradient-based training with noise influencing both spike timing and network dynamics.
neurips-2024-exact-gradients-for-stochas.tldr: A rough-path framework establishes sufficient conditions for exact gradients in noisy spiking networks and provides a differentiable training solver.

paragraphs: People may recognize the lighting or texture they want in an image without knowing how to describe it precisely. Reference images offer a natural way to communicate those preferences. This paper argues that treating their appearance as one broad style is too coarse, especially when users want different attributes from different sources.

The authors introduce FiVA, a dataset of one million generated images annotated with fine-grained visual attributes. Its organized taxonomy separates characteristics such as lighting, texture, and dynamics. This makes individual aspects of appearance explicit rather than grouping all visual choices into a single style description.

Using this dataset, the authors propose FiVA-Adapter, a framework that separates and transfers attributes from one or more reference images into a generated image. The intended benefit is selective customization: users can combine particular characteristics while retaining their desired content. The contribution joins a structured training resource with a method for more specific visual control, expanding the kinds of preferences users can express through image references.
neurips-2024-fiva-fine-grained-visual-at.tldr: FiVA provides annotated visual attributes and an adapter for selectively combining characteristics from reference images in image generation.

paragraphs: Fluent language generation does not by itself establish how well a model can plan. GameTraversalBenchmark examines planning through movement across diverse two-dimensional grid maps. The task gives models concrete objectives to traverse, making success depend on the actions they generate rather than solely on the plausibility of a written explanation.

Evaluation combines three concerns: completing the objectives, using few movement steps, and making few generation errors. These are joined in a composite measure called GTB_Score. This setup distinguishes reaching the requested locations from doing so efficiently and producing a usable sequence of actions, so the benchmark assesses several aspects of planning together.

Among the LLMs in the main evaluation, GPT-4-Turbo achieves the highest composite score at 44.97%. A preliminary test of the reasoning model o1 reaches 67.84%. The latter result suggests stronger performance is possible while supporting the authors' conclusion that the benchmark remains challenging. The scores describe performance on this particular combined evaluation of map traversal, efficiency, and generation accuracy.
neurips-2024-gametraversalbenchmark-eval.tldr: GameTraversalBenchmark tests LLM planning through grid navigation, scoring objective completion, route efficiency, and generation errors together.

paragraphs: Neural networks can perform well on tabular data, but their predictions are often difficult to explain directly from their architecture. This paper proposes mesomorphic networks, which combine a deep model with a linear prediction model for each individual input. The goal is to make explanations part of how predictions are produced.

A deep hypernetwork generates the parameters of the instance-specific linear model. The model used to make a prediction is therefore linear for that instance, while the process choosing its parameters has the flexibility of a deep network. This is the sense in which the architecture is both deep and linear: it does not rely on one fixed linear model for every example.

The authors report performance comparable to state-of-the-art tabular classifiers and better than existing methods designed to be explainable. Their results support the possibility of retaining strong predictive accuracy while producing interpretable models by construction. The empirical claim is about the evaluated tabular tasks, where generating a separate linear model for each instance provides the proposed link between flexibility and explanation.
neurips-2024-interpretable-mesomorphic-n.tldr: Mesomorphic networks use deep hypernetworks to generate interpretable linear models for individual tabular inputs while retaining strong empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: Assessing advanced historical knowledge is difficult because available information is uneven across places and periods. HiST-LLM addresses this problem with a benchmark based on a subset of the Seshat Global History Databank. Its source material spans every major world region from the Neolithic period to the Industrial Revolution.

The underlying structured historical resource contains 36,000 data points across 600 societies and more than 2,700 scholarly references, assembled and reviewed by experts and graduate research assistants. The authors evaluate seven models from the Gemini, OpenAI, and Llama families using questions with four answer choices. Balanced accuracy ranges from 33.6% for Llama-3.1-8B to 46% for GPT-4-Turbo, above the 25% random-guessing level.

The tested models perform better on earlier periods. Regional performance is more even, although the more advanced models do better in the Americas and worse in Oceania and Sub-Saharan Africa. The results indicate some expert-level historical knowledge, while falling short of expert comprehension. They also show why coverage across regions and periods matters when interpreting an overall history score.
neurips-2024-large-language-models-exper.tldr: HiST-LLM finds that tested language models answer expert-level global-history questions above chance but fall short of expert comprehension.

paragraphs: People choose their own learning goals, but the signals guiding those choices are not fully understood. One candidate is visible improvement in performance. This paper investigates an additional signal: latent learning progress, meaning improvement people infer from their actions and knowledge of the environment even when their immediate performance has not changed.

The researchers designed a hierarchical reinforcement learning task involving 175 participants. Participants repeatedly selected goals and learned policies tailored to those goals. This setup allowed the authors to examine goal choices alongside learning, using both behavioral evidence and computational models to test whether inferred progress influenced which goals people pursued.

The results support an influence of latent learning progress on goal selection. They also reveal differences between individuals, partly mediated by recognition of the task's hierarchical structure. This suggests that understanding how a task is organized can help shape the progress people perceive. The authors position the findings as a foundation for more personalized learning experiences and artificial agents that choose goals in more human-like ways.
neurips-2024-latent-learning-progress-dr.tldr: A human learning study finds that inferred progress, even without immediate performance gains, influences which goals people choose.

paragraphs: Broadcasting on trees studies how information about a root state survives as states propagate through a tree according to a Markov chain. The inference task is to recover information about the root from the leaves. Belief propagation achieves Bayes-optimal performance in linear time when counting real operations, yet that runtime can conceal other forms of computational complexity.

This paper studies a restricted but informative family of estimators: low-degree polynomials of the observations. The authors prove that, below the Kesten-Stigum bound, any polynomial with degree O(log N) has vanishing correlation with the root for a tree with N leaves. The result applies to any Markov chain in the stated broadcast setting.

Earlier results established polynomial-degree obstacles for particular chains; this work establishes the stated general result below the threshold. The conclusion limits what low-degree polynomial estimators can capture, rather than ruling out inference by every algorithm. The proof is also notable for handling a setting that is neither based on a product measure nor easily reduced to one.
neurips-2024-low-degree-hardness-for-bro.tldr: Below the Kesten-Stigum bound, logarithmic-degree polynomial estimators have vanishing correlation with the root in the studied tree-broadcast problem.

paragraphs: Symmetry gives machine learning a way to describe transformations that have known mathematical structure. Existing equivariant networks commonly build in predefined representations of those transformations. MatrixNet instead learns matrix representations of group elements supplied as inputs, making the representation itself part of what the network learns for a prediction task.

The paper evaluates this architecture on tasks involving several finite groups and the Artin braid group. Across these evaluations, MatrixNet achieves better sample efficiency and generalization than several standard baselines. These findings concern learning over the tested groups, where the structure of the group provides relationships the model can use.

The authors also show that MatrixNet respects group relations and generalizes to elements with greater word length than those seen in training. Word length describes how long a sequence of basic group operations is needed in an expression. The result therefore connects learning algebraic relationships with handling longer compositions. The contribution is evidence that learned matrix representations can preserve useful group structure while supporting prediction beyond training-length examples.
neurips-2024-matrixnet-learning-over-sym.tldr: MatrixNet learns matrix representations of group elements and shows improved generalization, including to longer compositions than those used in training.

paragraphs: Molecular energy minimization depends on how a system's configurations are represented during optimization. Traditional coarse-graining reduces the number of degrees of freedom. This paper proposes a neural-network reparametrization that can adjust complexity more flexibly, including sometimes increasing it when doing so makes the optimization problem easier to solve.

The approach retains continuous access to fine-grained modes and avoids force-matching. Its framework allows potentially arbitrary neural-network architectures to define the reparametrization, including graph neural networks, while incorporating coarse-grained modes as needed. The central idea is to improve the representation through which optimization proceeds without requiring a strict reduction in the system's available detail.

In experiments with weak Lennard-Jones forces, the graph-neural-network version is the only tested model to find the correct configuration. In the reported protein-folding scenarios, it recovers target structures more accurately and converges faster to the deepest energy states than traditional optimization methods. These findings support flexible reparametrization as a useful route to improved energy minimization in the molecular settings studied.
neurips-2024-neural-network-reparametriz.tldr: Neural-network reparametrization improves molecular energy optimization by flexibly changing the representation while preserving access to fine-grained modes.

paragraphs: Estimating performance on unfamiliar data is difficult when its labels are unavailable. Agreement-on-the-line offers an approach based on how predictions from an ensemble relate to one another. This paper asks whether that relationship remains useful for foundation models, whose lightly fine-tuned copies may have less diversity than networks trained independently from scratch.

For multiple fine-tuning runs of one foundation model, the authors compare randomness from linear-head initialization, data order, and data subsets. These choices produce markedly different levels of agreement-on-the-line. Across the vision and language benchmarks studied, only random head initialization reliably induces the relationship among those tested sources of randomness.

The authors also find that ensembles of different foundation models, pretrained on different datasets and then fine-tuned on the same task, can exhibit the relationship. With carefully constructed diversity, agreement-based methods predict out-of-distribution performance with high precision in their evaluations. The practical lesson is that ensemble construction is central to making this form of prediction work; simply repeating fine-tuning does not reliably produce the needed behavior.
neurips-2024-predicting-the-performance-.tldr: Carefully chosen ensemble diversity enables agreement-based prediction of foundation-model performance on unlabeled out-of-distribution data.

paragraphs: Deeper parameterized quantum circuits can express more complex functions, but also accumulate more errors on noisy hardware. Additional parameters increase the measurements needed to evaluate gradients. Quantum Deep Equilibrium Models address this tension by bringing equilibrium-based learning to the task of training a parameterized quantum circuit.

A deep equilibrium model represents repeated application of a shared transformation through a fixed point found by a root solver. This mimics an infinite-depth network with tied weights without explicitly storing all its layers. The paper uses this idea as a training paradigm for quantum machine learning, seeking useful predictive behavior with shallower circuits.

The evaluations include four-class MNIST with four qubits, followed by ten-class tasks involving MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR. QDEQ is competitive with comparable baselines and outperforms a network with five times as many layers. These results show that the approach can reduce the circuit depth needed for the evaluated tasks, a relevant benefit when deeper circuits incur greater noise.
neurips-2024-quantum-deep-equilibrium-mo.tldr: Quantum deep equilibrium models achieve competitive classification results with shallower circuits by using fixed-point-based training.

paragraphs: Uniformity testing asks whether an unknown distribution assigns equal probability to n possible outcomes or is at least epsilon away from doing so in total variation distance. Standard methods need on the order of sqrt(n)/epsilon² samples. However, distributions between those two cases can produce inconsistent conclusions across repeated applications.

This paper requires replicability for arbitrary input distributions, including those intermediate cases. The authors construct a tester with sample complexity approximately sqrt(n)/(epsilon² rho), up to logarithmic factors, where rho controls the replicability requirement. The dependence on inverse rho is nearly linear, improving on the inverse-square overhead that replicability typically introduces.

The authors also prove a nearly matching lower bound for symmetric algorithms, whose outputs do not change when domain elements are relabeled. This class includes their method and all existing uniformity testers described in the abstract. The result therefore pairs a more sample-efficient replicable procedure with evidence that its sample requirements are close to unavoidable within this natural class of algorithms.
neurips-2024-replicable-uniformity-testi.tldr: A replicable uniformity tester achieves nearly linear inverse dependence on the replicability parameter, with a nearly matching lower bound for symmetric algorithms.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models use the fixed point of a repeatedly applied, shared-weight transformation as their predictive representation. This paper studies what that construction can express and which solutions its learning dynamics favor. It aims to give theoretical explanations for advantages that have previously been observed empirically.

The authors establish separations between equilibrium models and fully connected feedforward networks under specified restrictions on depth, width, and parameter magnitudes. One result concerns a width-m equilibrium model and feedforward approximations of depth O(m^alpha), for alpha between zero and one. Another shows efficient approximation of certain steep functions by equilibrium models, while the compared bounded-depth feedforward networks require exponentially large weight magnitudes.

The paper also characterizes the implicit regularization produced by gradient flow in a diagonal linear equilibrium model, with examples illustrating its benefits. These results distinguish representational efficiency from the preferences introduced by training. Based on the analysis and empirical validation, the authors conjecture potential advantages for learning certain high-frequency components; they present that broader interpretation as a conjecture rather than a general theorem.
neurips-2024-separation-and-bias-of-deep.tldr: The paper establishes conditional expressivity advantages and learning biases of deep equilibrium models, suggesting possible benefits for certain high-frequency functions.

paragraphs: Online classifiers update as examples arrive, making them useful for large streams and throughput-sensitive applications. Rapid correction after errors can also make them vulnerable to outliers. An unusual example near the end of a stream may trigger an excessive update, leaving the final model much less accurate than earlier versions.

The proposed method keeps a fixed-size collection of intermediate models using weighted reservoir sampling. Its quality signal is how long a model survives without making an error: more passive rounds suggest a better solution. The reservoir retains K previous weight vectors, favoring those with longer survival times, and combines them into an ensemble.

This stabilization requires no additional data passes, hold-out set, or memory that grows with the stream. Experiments with Passive-Aggressive classification and First-Order Sparse Online Learning show consistent, significant improvements over the unmodified methods. A theoretical result also bounds the ensemble's risk in relation to the underlying algorithm's regret. The method uses the history already produced during online learning to reduce dependence on its final update.
neurips-2024-stabilizing-linear-passive-.tldr: Weighted reservoir sampling stabilizes online classifiers by ensembling intermediate models that remain error-free for longer.

paragraphs: Kernel Kullback-Leibler divergence compares probability distributions through covariance operators in a kernel feature space. It applies a quantum form of KL divergence to these representations, instead of directly comparing probability-density ratios. This paper studies the statistical and geometric behavior of that approach and addresses a restriction in its original definition.

The original divergence cannot be defined for distributions with disjoint supports. The authors introduce a regularized version that is well defined for all distributions. They derive bounds on how far this modification deviates from the original divergence, along with concentration bounds that characterize its statistical behavior.

For distributions represented by finite point sets, the paper provides a closed-form expression that makes the regularized quantity implementable. It also derives a Wasserstein gradient descent scheme for discrete distributions and empirically studies moving a collection of points toward a target distribution. The work therefore connects mathematical control of regularization with concrete computation and distribution transport, extending where this kernel-based comparison can be used.
neurips-2024-statistical-and-geometrical.tldr: A regularized kernel KL divergence handles disjoint supports and comes with statistical bounds, a finite-sample formula, and a transport scheme.

paragraphs: Reducing data to a few dimensions can reveal structure, but a single global map may distort relationships. The PCA tree instead organizes dimensionality reduction hierarchically, using different local linear representations in different regions. Like an autoencoder, it provides explicit mappings both into the reduced representation and back to the original space.

Projection uses a sparse oblique tree: each hard split is defined by a hyperplane involving only a few features, and the leaves apply linear mappings. Reconstruction also uses local linear mappings. This combination makes the model interpretable and allows new points to be projected or reconstructed quickly.

Training all tree parameters jointly is nonconvex and nondifferentiable. The authors propose an algorithm guaranteed to decrease error monotonically and report that it scales to large datasets without approximation. Experiments on image and document datasets reveal varied low-dimensional and cluster structure. The approach offers a hierarchy of local views together with reconstruction, while the optimization guarantee concerns decreasing error rather than finding a global optimum.
neurips-2024-the-tree-autoencoder-model-.tldr: PCA trees provide interpretable hierarchical dimensionality reduction through local linear projections and reconstructions, trained with monotonically decreasing error.

paragraphs: Transformers benefit from substantial pretraining investment, but quadratic-time self-attention can make inference costly. State space models offer subquadratic alternatives, yet have received less pretraining compute than the strongest Transformers. MOHAWK transfers knowledge from a pretrained Transformer into a different architecture so that the alternative can benefit from that existing investment.

The method views both architectures as mixing information across tokens through matrices. Distillation proceeds at three levels: first matching these mixing matrices, then matching hidden units within blocks, and finally matching whole-model predictions. This progression connects internal information processing to the outputs the student ultimately needs to produce.

The authors use MOHAWK to build Phi-Mamba, a Mamba-2 variant based on Phi-1.5, using three billion tokens. They report using less than 1% of the data typically required for training from scratch while outperforming all earlier open-source non-Transformer models in their comparison. The result demonstrates a route for transferring the benefits of Transformer pretraining into an architecture with different computational scaling.
neurips-2024-transformers-to-ssms-distil.tldr: MOHAWK progressively distills Transformer internals and predictions into a state space model using a small fraction of typical pretraining data.

paragraphs: Adding image capabilities to a language model can weaken its ability to follow instructions containing only text. Wings studies this forgetting through attention patterns across layers. The authors find a relationship between text-only forgetting and a shift of attention from text before an image to text after it.

Their response is to add Low-Rank Residual Attention blocks alongside each layer's main attention block. These modality learners expand the trainable space and compensate for attention shifts, using low-rank connections for efficiency. Visual learners first participate in aligning images and text; textual learners are added later, with token-wise routing combining the learners' outputs.

This parallel arrangement gives visual and textual learning complementary roles during multimodal training. The authors report that Wings outperforms equally scaled multimodal models on both text-only tasks and visual question answering. The findings support compensating for attention changes as a way to address text-only forgetting while expanding visual capabilities, and connect the architectural intervention to an observed change in how the model attends to its inputs.
neurips-2024-wings-learning-multimodal-l.tldr: Wings adds complementary low-rank attention learners to improve multimodal abilities while addressing text-only forgetting.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples using a learned denoiser, but sampling can visit regions far outside the denoiser's training distribution. The paper identifies inaccurate denoising in those regions as a fundamental source of degraded sample quality. The issue is especially pronounced in parallel sampling, where an entire trajectory is initialized and updated together.

The authors observe that a diffusion model implicitly defines a log-likelihood ratio for distinguishing distributions with different amounts of added noise. That expression depends on denoiser behavior beyond its standard training distribution. They turn this observation into a self-supervised contrastive objective that teaches the model to distinguish noise levels.

The extra objective improves denoising outside the usual training distribution. Experiments show benefits for both sequential and parallel sampling, with significant improvements in the performance and speed of parallel samplers. The contribution connects a classification interpretation of diffusion models to a training change aimed at the states encountered during generation, especially when sampling procedures make many out-of-distribution evaluations.
neurips-2024-your-diffusion-model-is-sec.tldr: Contrastive training that distinguishes noise levels improves out-of-distribution denoising and boosts sequential and parallel diffusion sampling.
